anatomy.intro: Rounded rib segments and substantial curved spines give this cactus its heavy-built outline.

parts.function: The raised green ridge is part of the photosynthetic stem.
parts.label: Broad rib

parts.function: A rounded swelling divides the rib into a series of prominent segments.
parts.label: Chin-like tubercle

parts.function: The pale growing cushion carries a cluster of spines.
parts.label: Woolly areole

parts.function: A stout, curved spine projects beyond the green body from the areole.
parts.label: Curved spine

flowers.text: Pale pink funnels are about 2 cm across in the RHS description. Their small scale contrasts with the broad ribbed body and heavy spines.

growth.note: The broad ribs divide into rounded tubercles as the body enlarges, giving the older plant its strongly sculpted surface.

stages.text: The young cactus is broad and relatively flattened.
stages.title: Low globe

stages.text: The ribs and their rounded segments become more substantial as the plant enlarges.
stages.title: Heavier body

stages.text: Mature plants can carry small funnels around the upper body.
stages.title: Flowering adult

habitat.text: This is a northwestern Argentine species; Kew places it in the subtropical biome. Its broad green or bluish stem and stout spines belong to a succulent subshrub, despite the common name giant chin cactus. The regional origin helps distinguish it from the smaller Paraguay-associated moon cactus sharing its genus in this collection.

lookalikes.name: Variegated moon cactus
lookalikes.text: Both have notched Gymnocalycium ribs, but giant chin cactus develops broader tubercles and much stouter spines than the smaller moon cactus.

mature.text: RHS lists a cultivated spread of 10–50 cm. The rounded body can carry 10–30 or more tubercled ribs, each lined with stout curved spines.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Costa Farms.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: Kew traces the species to Echinocactus saglionis, published in 1847, with the Gymnocalycium combination following in 1922. Older reference names refer to the same botanical history.
